For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Equality of measures is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; by [F2], $\sim$ is therefore an equivalence relation, so each class $[\theta]_\sim$ is defined.
If $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$, then $P_\theta=P_\eta$ gives $\bar\psi(P_\theta)=\bar\psi(P_\eta)$ and hence $\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)$. Thus (iii) implies identifiability.

Suppose $\psi$ is identifiable. Form the relation $G:=\{(Q,a):\text{there exists }\theta\in\Theta\text{ with }Q=P_\theta\text{ and }a=\psi(\theta)\}$. Every $Q\in\mathcal M$ has at least one such parameter by [F1]. If both $\theta$ and $\eta$ represent the same $Q$, then [F2] gives $\theta\sim\eta$, so [F4] gives $\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)$. Thus $G$ has exactly one value for each $Q\in\mathcal M$, defines a function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$ by [F3], and satisfies $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$. This construction defines the graph directly and uses no choice axiom.

By [F2], $\eta\in[\theta]_\sim$ exactly when $\eta\sim\theta$. If $a,b\in[\theta]_\sim$, then $a\sim\theta$ and $b\sim\theta$, so symmetry and transitivity from step 1.1 give $a\sim b$; conversely, $\theta\sim\eta$ gives $\eta\in[\theta]_\sim$. Hence [F4] is exactly constancy of $\psi$ on every class.

If $\bar\psi_1$ and $\bar\psi_2$ both factor $\psi$, each $Q\in\mathcal M$ equals $P_\theta$ for some $\theta$ by [F1], and then $\bar\psi_1(Q)=\psi(\theta)=\bar\psi_2(Q)$ by [F3]. The factor is unique. The implication in step 1.2 and the construction in step 1.3 give (i) iff (iii), while step 2.1 gives (i) iff (ii).

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

derivations.claim: The full power set contains $\mathcal X$ and is closed under finite unions and complements, so it is an algebra of subsets. Every countable union of its members is still a subset of $\mathcal X$, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F1] and gives a measurable space by [F2]. For any $p\in[0,1]$, both singleton masses $p$ and $1-p$ are nonnegative, and $P_p(\mathcal X)=p+(1-p)=1$. If $(A_n)$ is pairwise disjoint, each of $0$ and $1$ belongs to at most one $A_n$, so $\sum_nP_p(A_n)=p\mathbf1_{\{1\in\cup_nA_n\}}+(1-p)\mathbf1_{\{0\in\cup_nA_n\}}=P_p(\cup_nA_n)$. Hence every $P_p$ is a probability measure by [F3].

If $P_p=P_{p'}$, evaluation on $\{1\}$ gives $p=P_p(\{1\})=P_{p'}(\{1\})=p'$. Thus the model map is injective and equal laws force $\psi(p)=\psi(p')$; the target is identifiable by [F7]. By [F8] it factors uniquely through the set of Bernoulli laws.

derivations.claim: The full power set contains $\mathcal X$ and is closed under finite unions and complements, so it is an algebra of subsets. Every countable union of its members is still a subset of $\mathcal X$, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F1] and gives a measurable space by [F2]. For every $(u,v)\in\Theta$, both masses $u+v$ and $1-u-v$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$. In a pairwise disjoint sequence of events, each singleton $\{0\}$ and $\{1\}$ appears at most once, so the displayed formula is countably additive. Thus $P_{u,v}$ is a probability measure by [F3], and the family is an experiment by [F4].

The points $(u,v)=(1/5,1/2)$ and $(u',v')=(3/10,2/5)$ have coordinates in $[0,1]$, and their sums are $1/5+1/2=2/10+5/10=7/10$ and $3/10+2/5=3/10+4/10=7/10\le1$, so both belong to $\Theta$. Both measures assign $7/10$ to $\{1\}$ and $3/10$ to $\{0\}$; the four events $\varnothing,\{0\},\{1\},\mathcal X$ consequently have probabilities $0,3/10,7/10,1$ under both laws, so $P_{u,v}=P_{u',v'}$. But $\psi(u,v)=1/5\ne3/10=\psi(u',v')$. By [F7], $\psi$ is not identifiable; by [F8], it cannot factor through the model-law set.
